steps: This video shows how a Claude Code hook blocks a dangerous command before it runs. The CLAUDE dot md file auto-loads, and a developer asks Claude Code to wipe the stale build folder.
Claude picks rm dash r f dot slash build. That is risky, and a prompt that only says be careful could still let it through.
Your settings dot json in the dot claude folder routes every Bash tool call to a PreToolUse hook first, using the matcher Bash. The hook watches for patterns like rm dash r f and drop table.
The hook script, check bash dot j s, inspects the command in the tool input, finds rm dash r f, and returns deny. The call is blocked.
Bash never executes. Claude Code is told why it was denied, and passes the reason back to the developer: destructive command blocked.
Claude narrows the command to remove only the log files in build. The hook sees nothing destructive and returns an empty object, which means allowed.

Only the allowed call reaches the shell, and it runs. The takeaway: code in a hook enforces the rule every time, where a prompt can only ask. The full walkthrough is in the Gennoor Claude certification course.
